sections.heading: C — Impaired driving
sections.markdown:
## C — Impaired driving (part one)

FACT_ID: sec05-F01 | anchor: A01
Alcohol mixed with driving is one of the greatest factors in highway crashes, and studies cited by the handbook show that about twenty-eight percent of recent fatal crashes in West Virginia involved drivers who had been driving under the influence of alcohol [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F02 | anchor: A01
Adults are not the only drivers responsible for alcohol-related fatal crashes, because drivers under twenty-one years of age are involved in them as well [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F03 | anchor: A01
Alcohol reduces alertness, interferes with judgment and impairs vision [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F04 | anchor: A01
Alcohol affects a person differently at different times, because physical and emotional conditions, other drugs or even the amount of food in the stomach can change its effect [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F05 | anchor: A01
Physical exercise, black coffee, fresh air, cold showers and other home remedies do not effectively sober a person up, and time is the only sobering influence [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F06 | anchor: A01
A one-ounce shot of one-hundred-proof whiskey, a six-ounce glass of wine and a twelve-ounce can of beer all contain the same amount of alcohol [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F07 | anchor: A01
Drinking affects judgment, so decisions made under the influence of alcohol reflect impeded judgment [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F08 | anchor: A01
The legal drinking age in West Virginia is twenty-one, and under the zero tolerance law a driver under twenty-one found with any measurable amount of alcohol in the system will lose the driver's license [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F09 | anchor: A01
A designated driver, the most reasonable, safe and practical way to avoid drinking and driving, is a selected or volunteer companion who will not drink alcohol while responsible for driving friends home, and should be appointed before any activity involving alcohol begins [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F10 | anchor: A01
In West Virginia a blood alcohol concentration above point zero five percent and below point zero eight percent is relevant evidence to presume that the driver's ability is impaired, a concentration of point zero eight percent or more creates a presumption of driving under the influence, and the license can be revoked even when the concentration is below point zero eight percent [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

FACT_ID: sec05-F11 | anchor: A01
Drinking more than one drink per hour builds the blood alcohol level, and the handbook's example shows the level still rising after a last drink at eleven thirty at night and remaining above point zero six percent at four in the morning, enough for a DUI arrest [A01].
Source: [A01 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0031]

sections.heading: C — Impaired driving
sections.markdown:
## C — Impaired driving (part two)

FACT_ID: sec05-F12 | anchor: A02
Driving while using drugs is very dangerous with effects like those of drinking, because drugs, even prescribed or bought over the counter, can cause drowsiness, loss of coordination, hallucinations or total body malfunctions, and alcohol combined with drugs can be deadly [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F13 | anchor: A02
A driver arrested for DUI is subject to the implied consent law and is deemed to have consented to the designated breath test for alcohol content, and refusing that test brings revocation of the driving privilege for one year and up to life [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F14 | anchor: A02
The implied consent law does not mean a fine or jail for having alcohol on the breath, rather it protects a driver who has not been drinking because the test gives a medically accepted measure, and it safeguards the public by arresting those who refuse to be tested [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F15 | anchor: A02
A DUI offense by a driver under eighteen results in revocation until the age of eighteen or for the applicable statutory period, whichever is longer, and until all other requirements are met [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F16 | anchor: A02
Whenever a license is revoked or suspended for DUI, the driver must complete a prescribed Safety and Treatment program before becoming eligible for reinstatement [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F17 | anchor: A02
A first zero tolerance offense by a driver under twenty-one with any measurable alcohol carries a fine of twenty-five to one hundred dollars, no jail, and a minimum revocation of thirty days [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F18 | anchor: A02
A second zero tolerance offense carries a fine of one hundred to five hundred dollars, twenty-four hours in jail, and a minimum revocation of sixty days or until the eighteenth birthday, whichever is greater [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F19 | anchor: A02
A first DUI with alcohol or drugs at a blood alcohol concentration below point one five, or knowingly permitting DUI, carries a fine of one hundred to five hundred dollars, jail of up to six months, and a minimum revocation of fifteen days [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F20 | anchor: A02
A first DUI at a blood alcohol concentration of point one five or more carries a fine of two hundred to one thousand dollars, jail of two days to six months, and a minimum revocation of forty-five days [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F21 | anchor: A02
DUI with child endangerment carries a fine of two hundred to one thousand dollars, jail of forty-eight hours to twelve months, and a minimum revocation of sixty days [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F22 | anchor: A02
DUI with bodily injury carries a fine of two hundred to one thousand dollars, jail of twenty-four hours to twelve months, and a minimum revocation of sixty days [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F23 | anchor: A02
DUI with serious bodily injury carries a fine of up to three thousand dollars, jail of two to ten years, and a minimum revocation of sixty days [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F24 | anchor: A02
DUI with death is a felony carrying jail of five to thirty years and a lifetime revocation [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F25 | anchor: A02
A second DUI offense carries a fine of one thousand to three thousand dollars, jail of six to twelve months, and a minimum revocation of one year [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F26 | anchor: A02
A third or subsequent DUI offense carries a fine of three thousand to five thousand dollars, jail of one to three years, and a minimum revocation of one year [A02].
Source: [A02 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0032]

FACT_ID: sec05-F27 | anchor: A03
A DUI or DUI-related event places a revocation on the driving record, and when alcohol was involved the driver may join the Interlock Program, which allows legal driving only in a vehicle fitted with an ignition interlock device that prevents an intoxicated person from starting the car [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F28 | anchor: A03
Interlock participation is an option for some DUI offenders and mandatory for others depending on the offense, and a driver revoked for two or more DUI or related offenses within a ten-year period must participate [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F29 | anchor: A03
A driver whose Interlock application is approved before the scheduled revocation begins does not serve a minimum revocation period and can install the device immediately, while a driver who applies late may have to serve the minimum revocation and still complete the program [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F30 | anchor: A03
Drowsy driving is impaired driving, because after being awake for about eighteen hours driving skills become comparable to those of someone under the influence of drugs or alcohol, reaction time slows and crash risk rises [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F31 | anchor: A03
A drowsy driver responds more slowly to road and traffic conditions, struggles to process complex information from several places at once, grows careless in driving decisions, has trouble paying attention and may fall asleep at the wheel [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F32 | anchor: A03
The best way to reduce drowsiness is more sleep, and a drowsy driver should not drive but pull over to a safe area for a short nap, since as little as ten to twenty minutes of sleep can make a big difference [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F33 | anchor: A03
Drivers should avoid driving at the times they feel sleepy, often early morning, late afternoon or night, and should let a well-rested person drive, carpool, use public transportation, call a taxi or ask a family member or friend to drive [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F34 | anchor: A03
Another driver may be drowsy when the head nods or drops, the vehicle drifts out of the lane, crosses edge or center lines or hits rumble strips, there are near misses especially rear-end, speed varies erratically with weaving, or the vehicle rear-ends another, hits one head-on or strikes a stationary object [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]

FACT_ID: sec05-F35 | anchor: A03
Signs that you yourself are drowsy include falling asleep at stop lights, yawning, rubbing the eyes, watery eyes, heavy eyelids, not remembering the last few miles, missing road signs or exits, unplanned lane changes, head nodding and driving off the road or onto the rumble strips [A03].
Source: [A03 -> src:rdmv-wv-class-e:west-virginia-division-of-motor-vehicles:handbook:pdf-0033]
